original_text: Transport in Vertebrates Comparison of Circulatory Pathways Fish -Blood flows in single loop Single atrium and single ventricle Amphibians -Blood flows in double loop Systemic circuit and pulmonary circuit Two atria with a single ventricle Other vertebrates -Blood flows in a double loop Heart divided by septum into separate sides
explanation: Vertebrate circulatory pathways vary: 1) Fish: have a single-loop pathway, where blood is pumped from a single ventricle to the gills, then to body tissues, and back to a single atrium. 2) Amphibians: have a double-loop pathway (systemic and pulmonary circuits) and a three-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle, which leads to some blood mixing. 3) Other vertebrates (birds and mammals): have a double-loop pathway and a four-chambered heart fully divided by a septum into separate left and right sides, preventing blood mixing.

questions.q: What type of circulatory pathway and heart structure is found in fish?
opts: Double loop; two atria and a single ventricle
Single loop; single atrium and single ventricle
Double loop; heart divided by a septum
questions.exp: Fish possess a single-loop circulatory pathway powered by a two-chambered heart consisting of one atrium and one ventricle.

questions.q: How does the heart of an amphibian differ from that of a mammal?
opts: Amphibians have a two-chambered heart, while mammals have a three-chambered heart.
Amphibians have a three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) with some blood mixing, whereas mammals have a four-chambered heart divided by a septum.
Amphibians have a closed system, while mammals have an open system.
Amphibians have only a systemic circuit, while mammals have only a pulmonary circuit.
questions.exp: Amphibians have a three-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle, which allows oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix. Mammals have a four-chambered heart divided by a septum, keeping the blood streams separate.
